Image Processing Microservice - HLD

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Intermediate–Advanced
Prerequisites: Message Queues, Object Storage, and Scalability
Asked at: Amazon, Google, Cloudinary, imgix, Shopify, Flipkart

TL;DR

An async image processing service that accepts image transformation jobs (resize, compress, format convert, watermark, thumbnail), executes them through a scalable worker pool, and delivers results via webhook or polling. Presigned URLs handle large uploads without proxying bytes through the API.💡 A presigned URL is a temporary link that carries its own permission to write one specific location in object storage. The client uploads straight to storage with it, so gigabytes of image never travel through our servers.

In 3 sentences: Clients upload images to S3 via presigned URLs, then submit a job describing which operations to chain (resize → compress → convert). The API enqueues to SQS/Kafka; stateless workers pull jobs, stream images through libvips, write outputs back to S3, and fire a webhook. Auto-scaling on queue depth keeps latency low without wasting compute.

Functional Requirements

Core (top 3)

  1. Submit a processing job — client uploads an image and specifies a pipeline of operations (resize, compress, format convert, watermark, thumbnail generation).
  2. Execute the pipeline — workers process operations in sequence, streaming the image through each step, and store the result in object storage.
  3. Retrieve results — client polls job status or receives a webhook callback with the output URL on completion.💡 A webhook is an HTTP endpoint the client publishes so we can call them the moment the job finishes, rather than them asking us repeatedly. It only works if the client is a reachable server, which is why the polling option stays.

Below the line

  • Real-time image transformations via URL path (like imgix/Cloudinary on-the-fly).
  • AI-powered operations (background removal, super-resolution, face detection).
  • Video processing or animated GIF pipelines.
  • Multi-region replication of output assets.
  • Batch ZIP download of multiple processed images.

Non-Functional Requirements

Core

  • Throughput — sustain 1000 images/sec at steady state, avg 2 MB per image.
  • Latency — P95 processing time < 5s for a standard resize+compress pipeline on a 2 MB JPEG.💡 P95 = the figure 95% of jobs come in under, so it describes the unluckiest 1 in 20 rather than the average. Averages hide the slow tail that users actually complain about. Learn more →
  • Idempotency — identical jobs (same source + same operations) return cached results, never re-process.💡 Idempotency = submitting the same work twice has the same effect as submitting it once. Here it is about money rather than correctness: a duplicate submission would cost us a second resize of an identical photo.
  • Availability — 99.9% uptime; no single component failure causes job loss.

Below the line

  • Sub-100ms latency for CDN-served on-the-fly transforms (out of scope, separate edge service).
  • Exactly-once delivery (we do at-least-once + idempotency).💡 At-least-once means the queue would rather hand a job to two workers than risk losing it, so duplicates are expected. Pairing that with idempotency is how you get an exactly-once effect without needing exactly-once delivery, which is not buildable over an unreliable network. Learn more →
  • Cross-region active-active processing.

Core Entities

  • Job — a processing request: source image reference, ordered list of operations, status, output location, retry count.
  • Operation — a single transformation step: type (resize, compress, convert, watermark, thumbnail), parameters (width, height, quality, format, position).
  • Pipeline — ordered sequence of operations applied to one source image. Executed left-to-right.
  • Output — the processed image stored in S3 with metadata (size, format, dimensions).
  • Tenant — the API consumer. Rate limits, quotas, and webhook URLs are scoped per tenant.
  • Worker — a stateless process that pulls jobs, runs the pipeline, and reports results.

API / System Interface

POST   /v1/upload-url              -> { presigned_url, source_key }
POST   /v1/jobs                    -> Job
GET    /v1/jobs/{id}               -> Job + output URL
BASH

POST /v1/upload-url

// Request
{ "filename": "product-hero.jpg", "content_type": "image/jpeg", "size_bytes": 2048000 }

// Response
{ "presigned_url": "https://bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/abc123?X-Amz-...",
  "source_key": "uploads/abc123/product-hero.jpg",
  "expires_in_seconds": 300 }
JSON

POST /v1/jobs

// Request
{ "source_key": "uploads/abc123/product-hero.jpg",
  "operations": [
    { "type": "resize", "width": 800, "height": 600, "fit": "cover" },
    { "type": "compress", "quality": 80 },
    { "type": "convert", "format": "webp" }
  ],
  "webhook_url": "https://myapp.com/hooks/image-done" }

// Response
{ "job_id": "job_7f2a9c", "status": "PENDING", "created_at": "2026-08-17T10:00:00Z" }
JSON

GET /v1/jobs/{id}

{ "job_id": "job_7f2a9c", "status": "COMPLETED",
  "output_url": "https://cdn.example.com/outputs/job_7f2a9c.webp",
  "completed_at": "2026-08-17T10:00:03Z" }
JSON

Security notes:

  • Presigned URLs scoped to specific key, expire in 5 minutes.
  • API authenticated via API key or JSON Web Token (JWT) per tenant.💡 A JWT is a signed token that proves which tenant is calling, so quotas, rate limits and webhook URLs can be attributed to the right customer. Learn more →
  • Source images never proxied through the API — clients upload directly to S3.

High-Level Design

FR-1: Submit a processing job

Components introduced:

  1. Processing API — validates the request, generates presigned URLs, and records jobs.
  2. S3 (source bucket) — holds uploaded source images. Clients write directly via presigned URL.
  3. Postgres (jobs table) — durable record of every job and its state.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Client requests a presigned upload URL from the API.
  2. Client uploads the raw image directly to S3 — the API never touches the bytes.
  3. Client submits POST /v1/jobs with the source_key and an operations array.
  4. API inserts a new job row in Postgres with status PENDING.
  5. Return 201 Created with the job_id.

Why presigned URLs? At 1000 images/sec × 2 MB average, that’s 2 GB/s of bandwidth. Proxying through the API would require enormous network capacity, and the API would spend all of its time as a pipe. Presigned URLs let S3 absorb the upload traffic directly, which is the one decision here that is not deferrable — no amount of worker tuning recovers from putting 2 GB/s through an application tier.

What we have deliberately left broken. A job can be submitted and is durably recorded. One thing step 4 does not do:

It accepts every submission as new work. A client that retries a POST /v1/jobs because the response timed out gets a second job for the identical source image and identical operations, and we will happily resize the same photo twice and charge ourselves for both. Retries are not an edge case here — the client is a mobile app on a flaky network, and the whole point of a job API is that submission and completion are separated, which is exactly the window in which a client gives up and tries again. That is Deep Dive 2.

FR-2: Execute the pipeline

New components:

  1. SQS Job Queue — decouples submission from processing. Visibility timeout ensures at-least-once delivery.
    💡 Visibility timeout = after a worker receives a message, it becomes invisible to other workers for N seconds. If the worker doesn’t delete it (crashes), the message reappears for another worker to retry.
  2. Worker Pool — a fixed set of stateless processes that pull from SQS, run the image pipeline with ImageMagick, and write outputs to S3.
  3. S3 (output bucket) — stores processed images. Separate from source bucket for lifecycle policies.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. API sends a message to SQS containing { job_id, source_key, operations }.
  2. Worker long-polls SQS with ReceiveMessage. Visibility timeout set to 60s.💡 Long polling means the worker’s request waits at the queue for up to 20 seconds for work to appear, instead of returning “nothing” instantly and being retried in a tight loop. Fewer wasted calls, and a job is picked up the moment it arrives.
  3. Worker downloads the source image from S3 into a streaming buffer.
  4. Worker runs the operations with ImageMagick: source → resize → compress → convert.
  5. Worker uploads output to S3 (output bucket, keyed by job_id).
  6. Worker updates Postgres: status = COMPLETED, output_url, completed_at.
  7. Worker deletes the SQS message (acknowledges success).
  8. If worker crashes, visibility timeout expires after 60s, message reappears for another worker.

What we have deliberately left broken. Jobs get executed, and a crashed worker’s job comes back rather than vanishing. Three things about this pipeline do not hold up:

  • The worker pool is a fixed size. Image traffic is spiky — a product launch, a bulk import, a timezone waking up — and a fixed pool is either idle most of the day or the queue backs up for hours. Sized for peak it wastes money; sized for average it misses the latency target exactly when load arrives. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • A message that keeps failing comes back forever. Step 8 is a retry loop with no counter. A genuinely un-processable image — a corrupt file, an unsupported format, a 50,000-pixel-wide PNG — fails, reappears after 60s, fails again, and occupies a worker indefinitely while taking capacity from jobs that would succeed. That is Deep Dive 3.
  • ImageMagick decodes the entire image into memory before doing anything. That is fine for a 2MB photo and fatal for a large one, and it sets the per-worker memory ceiling and therefore how many workers fit on a machine. That is Deep Dive 4.

Why SQS over Kafka here? SQS’s per-message visibility timeout is a natural fit for image processing where each job takes 1-5s. No partition management needed. For 10K+ images/sec, Kafka with consumer groups is the better choice.

FR-3: Retrieve results

New components:

  1. Webhook Dispatcher — async service that fires HTTP callbacks to the client’s registered URL on job completion.
  2. CDN — fronts the output S3 bucket for low-latency delivery of processed images.💡 A CDN (content delivery network) caches the finished images on servers near whoever is viewing them, so the output bucket is read once per region rather than once per viewer. Learn more →

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Worker completes processing, updates Postgres with COMPLETED status and output URL.
  2. Worker publishes a completion event to the webhook dispatcher.
  3. Webhook dispatcher POSTs to the client’s webhook_url with { job_id, status, output_url }.
  4. If webhook delivery fails, retries with exponential backoff (1s, 5s, 30s, 2min) up to 5 attempts.💡 Exponential backoff doubles the wait between attempts, so a client whose server is restarting gets time to come back instead of being hit five times in five seconds. Learn more →
  5. Client can also poll GET /v1/jobs/{id} at any time to check status.
  6. Output images are served through a CDN for low-latency global access.

Why both a webhook and a poll endpoint? Because a webhook requires the client to be a reachable server, and most callers are not — a mobile app or a browser has no URL we can POST to. The webhook is the efficient path for backend integrations; the poll is the fallback that always works. Offering only one of them excludes a whole class of caller.

What we have deliberately left broken. Clients learn about completion promptly and can always ask. Two things remain open:

  • Step 4 gives up after 5 attempts and nothing records that it did. A client whose endpoint was down for ten minutes is simply never told, and because the job itself succeeded there is no failure anywhere to investigate — the result sits in S3 that nobody knows about. A webhook that silently stops retrying is indistinguishable from one that was never fired.
  • Nothing here bounds how long an output lives. Processed images accumulate in the output bucket forever, and at 1000 images/sec that is a storage line item with no ceiling. The source bucket has the same problem once the job is done with it.

Technology Choices

Tier / Purpose Primary Alternatives Why
API Gateway Node.js or Go HTTP service FastAPI, Spring Boot Lightweight; handles presigned URL generation and job submission
Object Storage AWS S3 GCS, Azure Blob, MinIO Presigned URL uploads, cheap at-rest storage for source and output images
Job Queue SQS with visibility timeout Kafka, RabbitMQ, Google Pub/Sub Managed, per-message visibility timeout for retry, built-in DLQ
Job Metadata PostgreSQL MySQL, CockroachDB ACID for job state, indexed queries for status polling
Idempotency Cache Redis Memcached, DynamoDB Sub-ms hash lookups; TTL-based expiry for cache entries
Image Processing libvips ImageMagick, Sharp (Node bindings to libvips), Pillow Streaming architecture — 4-8x faster than ImageMagick, 1/10th memory
Auto-scaling K8s HPA on custom metrics AWS Auto Scaling, KEDA Scale workers on queue depth metric, not CPU
Dead-letter Queue SQS DLQ Kafka DLQ topic, RabbitMQ dead-letter exchange Isolate poison messages after max retries
Webhook Delivery Async HTTP with retries SNS, EventBridge Direct callback to client with exponential backoff
scroll →

Why libvips over ImageMagick

ImageMagick loads the full image into memory (200+ MB for a 50 MP image). libvips uses a streaming tile-based pipeline — memory stays at ~50 MB regardless of image size. At 200 workers, that’s 40 GB vs 10 GB total.

Data Modeling

Postgres (Job metadata — source of truth):

CREATE TABLE jobs (
    job_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    source_url TEXT NOT NULL,
    operations JSONB NOT NULL,
    idempotency_key VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    output_url TEXT,
    webhook_url TEXT,
    error_message TEXT,
    attempts INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    completed_at TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT uq_idempotency UNIQUE(tenant_id, idempotency_key)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_status ON jobs(status) WHERE status IN ('PENDING', 'PROCESSING');
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_tenant ON jobs(tenant_id, created_at DESC);
SQL

Redis (Idempotency cache + worker state):

Key: "idem:{hash}" → job_id (where hash = SHA256(source_url + canonical JSON of operations))
TTL: 24 hours

Key: "worker:{workerId}:heartbeat" → { job_id, started_at }
TTL: 30s

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Submit job Redis + Postgres Check idem cache → if miss, INSERT job row, enqueue
Poll job status Postgres SELECT status, output_url FROM jobs WHERE job_id = ?
Worker claims job SQS ReceiveMessage with visibility timeout
Worker completes Postgres + Redis UPDATE job status, SET idem cache with output URL
Detect stuck workers Redis TTL Heartbeat expires → message becomes visible again (SQS handles this)

Deep Dives

1) Image traffic is spiky and the pool is a fixed size. What drives the scaling signal?

The problem: Queue depth fluctuates wildly. E-commerce sites upload 10x more images during flash sales. Fixed worker counts either waste money (idle at baseline) or drop latency (overwhelmed at peak).

Bad — the fixed worker pool FR-2 built:
Provision for peak (200 workers) and eat the cost 24/7. At baseline (100 images/sec), 180 workers sit idle. Monthly cost: 200 × $150 = $30K in compute for maybe $5K worth of actual work.

Provision for peak (200 workers) and eat the cost 24/7. At baseline (100 images/sec), 180 workers sit idle. Monthly cost: 200 × $150 = $30K in compute for maybe $5K worth of actual work.

Scale workers based on CPU utilization (target 70%). Problem: image processing is bursty — by the time CPU spikes, the queue is already deep and latency has blown past the service level agreement (SLA). There’s a 2-3 minute lag between queue depth spiking and CPU reflecting it.

2) A client retries a timed-out submission. How do we not resize the same photo twice?

The problem: Clients retry on timeout. The same product image gets submitted with the same operations 3x. Without dedup, we waste compute processing it 3x and potentially confuse clients with multiple output URLs.

Bad — no dedup, which is what FR-1 shipped:
Every submission creates a new job. Three retries = three processing runs = 3x cost. Client gets three different job_ids and doesn’t know which output to use.

Every submission creates a new job. Three retries = three processing runs = 3x cost. Client gets three different job_ids and doesn’t know which output to use.

Add a unique index on . Second submission gets a constraint violation, API returns the existing job. Problem: this requires a Postgres round-trip on every submission, and under high concurrency you get lock contention on the index.

Sort keys alphabetically before hashing so and produce the same hash. This is critical — without canonicalization, semantically identical pipelines get different hashes.

3) One corrupt file retries forever and eats a worker. Where does a bad job go to die?

The problem: Workers crash (out-of-memory, or OOM, on a 200 MB TIFF), images are corrupt (truncated upload), operations are invalid (resize to 0×0). Without proper failure handling, jobs get stuck forever or retry infinitely.

Bad — the uncounted retry loop from FR-2 step 8:
Worker crashes, message reappears, next worker crashes on the same corrupt image. Repeat forever. The “poison message” consumes worker capacity and never completes.

Worker crashes, message reappears, next worker crashes on the same corrupt image. Repeat forever. The “poison message” consumes worker capacity and never completes.

Set on SQS. After 3 failures, message moves to a (DLQ). Problem: transient failures (S3 throttling) also end up in DLQ after just 3 attempts.

4) Decoding the whole image into memory caps how many workers fit on a box. What else works?

The problem: At 1000 images/sec, processing speed and memory usage directly determine infrastructure cost. The wrong library choice means 4x more servers.

Bad — the ImageMagick pipeline FR-2 built (load-all architecture):
Decompresses the entire image into memory. A 50 MP JPEG becomes ~288 MB of raw pixels. With 200 workers, that’s 57 GB of RAM just for pixel buffers. Workers need 4 GB each.

Decompresses the entire image into memory. A 50 MP JPEG becomes ~288 MB of raw pixels. With 200 workers, that’s 57 GB of RAM just for pixel buffers. Workers need 4 GB each.

Can do lazy loading for some formats, but resize still loads the full image. Better than ImageMagick, not optimal.

Core Flows

Flow 1: Submit Job

Walkthrough:

  1. Client gets a presigned URL and uploads directly to S3.
  2. Client submits the job. API hashes source + operations for idempotency.
  3. Redis cache hit → return existing result immediately (no reprocessing).
  4. Cache miss → create job, cache the hash, enqueue to SQS.

Non-obvious failure: If API crashes between Postgres INSERT and SQS SendMessage, the job is stuck as PENDING. A reconciliation job (runs every 5 min) detects jobs in PENDING for > 2 minutes and re-enqueues them.

Flow 2: Process Job

Walkthrough:

  1. Worker long-polls SQS. Receives a message with 60s visibility timeout.
  2. Marks job as PROCESSING in Postgres.
  3. Streams source image from S3 into libvips pipeline.
  4. Executes operations in sequence (resize → compress → convert) as one streaming pass.
  5. Uploads output to S3, updates job as COMPLETED, refreshes idempotency cache.
  6. Deletes SQS message and fires webhook to notify client.

Non-obvious failure: Worker takes > 60s (huge image). Visibility timeout expires, another worker picks up the same message. Solution: extend visibility timeout periodically (ChangeMessageVisibility every 30s while processing), and the idempotency cache prevents duplicate entries.

Final Architecture

The consolidated view after all deep dives — showing every component and how they connect:

Reading this diagram:

  • Client uploads directly to S3 (presigned URL), then submits a job to the API.
  • API checks Redis for idempotency, stores in Postgres, enqueues to SQS.
  • Workers pull from SQS, stream through libvips, write output to S3, update Postgres, fire webhook.
  • CDN fronts the output bucket for low-latency delivery.
  • Auto-scaler watches SQS queue depth and adjusts worker count.
  • DLQ (part of SQS) catches poison messages after max retries.

Interview Tips

  • Start with presigned URLs. Shows you understand bandwidth economics at scale (2 GB/s not proxied through API).
  • Mention idempotency early. Hash-based dedup prevents wasted compute — shows you think about real client retry behavior.
  • Know libvips vs ImageMagick cold. Streaming vs load-all mental model applies to any media processing system. This is a go-to follow-up.
  • Queue depth > CPU for scaling. CPU is a lagging indicator; queue depth is leading. This is the key auto-scaling insight.
  • DLQ is not optional. Every message-driven system needs a poison message strategy. Mention failure classification (transient vs permanent).
  • Derive the numbers: 1000 img/s × 5s processing = 5000 concurrent jobs. At 25 jobs/worker → ~200 workers steady state.
